query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their mechanical and thermoelastic behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory HEAs, the unusual temperature‐independent strength plateau and nearly isotropic thermoelastic behavior at high temperatures arise because local chemical disorder (i.e., random atomic-scale lattice distortions) lowers the activation barrier for edge dislocation motion. This lowering triggers a transition from screw‐dominated plasticity at low temperatures to an edge‐dominated regime at elevated temperatures, thereby sustaining the yield strength despite thermal softening.
generation.material_initial_state: A typical refractory high-entropy alloy such as NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 manufactured in two microstructural states: one with full random chemical disorder (maximally disordered state) and another with an induced partial short-range order (via controlled annealing) but with identical bulk composition.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the processing route (annealing/treatment conditions) to achieve differences in local chemical ordering while keeping overall composition constant. Then subject both variants to variable temperature mechanical testing (tensile/creep) combined with in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM to monitor dislocation core structures.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests under a range of temperatures (approximately 600 K to 1100 K) and controlled strain rates that are below the diffusion-limited regime; in situ characterization during deformation under identical loading and environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The degree of local atomic-scale lattice distortion and chemical disorder (or conversely, the presence of short-range ordering) mediates the dislocation core structure and consequently the active slip mechanism.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, conventional screw dislocation motion predominates, leading to high yield strength with typical thermal softening as temperature rises. However, in a highly disordered lattice, local misfit fluctuations reduce the energy required for edge dislocation activation. At elevated temperatures these fluctuations promote a gradual transition to edge-dominated motion, where thermal super-jogging and enhanced dislocation mobility are offset by strong local pinning. This unique balance results in a plateau in yield strength and reduced elastic anisotropy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The fully disordered alloy is expected to show an earlier and more pronounced transition to edge-dislocation dominated plasticity, with a clearly defined temperature range over which the yield strength remains nearly constant. In situ observations should reveal an increased proportion of edge dislocation segments at high temperatures in the fully disordered state relative to the partially ordered state. The partially ordered annealed variant, with less pronounced local fluctuations, should exhibit either a delayed or less dramatic transition, leading to a smaller or absent strength plateau.
generation.baseline: The standard processing (conventional annealing) condition that yields a fully random solid-solution microstructure and previously observed yield strength versus temperature behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for refractory HEAs tested in the temperature regime below the onset of diffusion-controlled softening (typically below ~0.5-0.6 Tm) and under strain rates where dislocation-based mechanisms dominate the deformation.
generation.uncertainty: While previous findings (e.g., PMC10453588::web::015::3_results and PMC8446014::web::015::theory_and_predictions_for_role_of_edge_) support edge dislocation control at high temperature, and studies like PMC10894205::web::016::discussion reveal conflicting interpretations regarding dislocation dominance, it remains uncertain how controlled variations in chemical ordering (short-range order versus full disorder) quantitatively affect the dislocation transition and overall thermoelastic response. This study directly targets this gap.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 samples: one processed to maximize random chemical disorder and another processed to promote partial short-range order via controlled annealing. Subject both sets to identical tensile and creep tests over 600–1100 K while conducting in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution TEM to capture dislocation core structures and monitor the ratio of edge to screw dislocations.
measurements: Yield strength versus temperature curves to identify the strength plateau region
In situ TEM/ND imaging to quantitatively assess the dislocation character (ratio of edge vs. screw segments) as a function of temperature
Lattice strain evolution profiles to verify isotropic elastic behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both microstructural variants exhibit the same temperature-dependent dislocation behavior and yield strength response—specifically, if no significant differences in the edge/screw transition or in the extent of the yield strength plateau are observed between the fully disordered and partially ordered states—then the hypothesis that local chemical disorder drives the transition to edge-dominated plasticity (and thus the strength plateau) is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In Figure 7, we compared the tensile strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA to that of other RHEAs [,,,,,,,], Ni-based superalloys [,,,], heat-resisting steels [], and refractory metals [] at extreme temperatures, demonstrating the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA’s promise for high-temperature applications. The yield strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was higher in comparison to that of typical RHEAs. When compared to some of the most widely used Ni-based superalloys, the tensile strength of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy was about 400 MPa higher than that of Haynes 230 and a little bit lower than Inconel 618 at the temperature range of RT-1073 K [Figure 5a]. Moreover, when the deformation temperature exceeded 1073 K, the strength of almost all metals and alloys dropped. This was due to the diffusion-controlled deformation mechanism activating above 0.5 to 0.6 Tm and softening the materials as a result []. Therefore, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA not only had a high melting point but also had a high strength without any complicated treatment, which means that it has good prospects for high-temperature applications.

Bulk and micropillar compression tests as a function of temperature and strain rate show the latter is plastically deformable in compression down to 77 K, but the former is not below room temperature. From our experimentally determined enthalpies of compression, the BDTT of VNbMoTaW is estimated to be 627 K (above room temperature) whereas that of TiZrNbHfTa is estimated to be 247 K (below room temperature) which indicates that high dislocation mobility at room temperature is one reason for the latter’s more ductile behavior. Consistent with this, deformation enthalpies and strength models both show kink migration is the rate-controlling step at room temperature in VNbTaMoW but not in TiZrNbHfTa. Another reason for the greater malleability of TiZrNbHfTa is the extremely low energy of screw dislocation cores in this RHEA compared with those in VNbMoTaW. Formation of the single BCC solid solution and the mechanical properties of the homogenization-treated NbTaTiV HEA at elevated temperatures The microstructure of the homogenized NbTaTiV refractory HEA was characterized, using the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) backscattered electron (BSE) technique, as shown in Fig. 1A. A typical simple solid-solution HEA microstructure with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm was identified without the presence of secondary phases or elemental segregations. The chemical composition of the sample was verified (using the point energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy analysis) to be Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8, indicating a homogeneous elemental distribution in a nearly equiatomic percentage. The measured ND patterns of the bulk samples, as illustrated in Fig. 1B, confirm the single BCC solid solution at RT and elevated temperatures. The lattice parameters of the present alloy at RT, 500°, 700°, and 900°C, which were determined by a single-peak fitting approach (), are 3.2318, 3.2445, 3.2511, and 3.2588 Å, respectively. cited_evidence.text: Figure 4b and c (see the Supplementary Note 7 for more details) show ~6,000,000 alloys with estimated strengths over 1 GPa at T = 1300 K, and ~1,300,000 over 2 GPa, far exceeding the strengths of any existing alloys. At 1300 K, many alloys also have strength/density >0.25 GPa g/cm3 (see Supplementary Note 7) that is the highest achieved to date at room temperature. We propose two super-high-strength/high-T alloys of Mo5W2.5CrZrHf and Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf for fabrication and testing, with predicted strengths of ~3 GPa at 1300 K. Preliminary thermodynamic assessment (Supplementary Note 8) suggests the use of low concentrations of Cr, Zr, and Hf to avoid intermetallic formation. We also propose two super-high-strength/high-T alloys, Mo6WCrZrHf and Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf with lower W, having predicted strengths of ~2.5 GPa at 1300 K. Future combinations of our design strategy with detailed thermodynamics, and added constraints (e.g., high ductility criterion) may lead to the discovery of new alloys that can achieve the multi-objective performance required in many critical engineering applications.
